      athletes are released to sport specifics at approximately 5 months postoperatively un-
      der the guidance of the surgeon, athletic trainer, and coaches. Again, it is emphasized
      by the treating surgeon that returning to sports can have detrimental effects on the
      outcome and success of this procedure and, therefore, it is highly recommended to
      refrain from collision or contact sports.
         Although evidence suggests that MAT is effective in relieving pain related to the loss
      of meniscal tissue, there are limited data on return to sport following this procedure.27
      Noyes and colleagues30 in 2004 assessed the outcomes of meniscal transplantation in
      38 patients younger than 50. Although not specifically evaluating “the athlete,” they
      did identify that 31 of 38 patients were unable to participate in sports activities preop-
      eratively, but at final follow-up (40 months) 29 of 38 patients had returned to higher-
      level activities to include swimming, biking, running, jumping, pivoting, and cutting.
      Of note, these patients were not released to light recreational sports until 12 months
      postoperatively, thus demonstrating a very conservative approach to rehabilitation. A
      2010 study by Alentorn-Geli and colleagues31 reported on 15 soccer players undergo-
      ing MAT and followed for an average of 36 months. Of the 14 patients available for
      follow-up, 12 had returned to play soccer at a mean of 7.6 months. They did not
      comment on their postoperative rehabilitation protocol. Last, Chalmers and col-
      leagues,29 in 2013, evaluated 13 athletes who were followed for a mean of 3.3 years
      after a meniscal allograft transplant. Of these, 10 returned to their previous sport, 9
      of whom returned at their desired level of play. Patients were released to full training

      SUMMARY

      In conclusion, athletes are a high-demand population, and when treating a meniscal
      injury, physicians must recognize how surgical decision making and postoperative
      rehabilitation protocols will affect the athlete’s career. Meniscectomy offers a fast re-
      turn to play with good short-term results, but the long-term risk of osteoarthritis must
      be weighed when making the appropriate patient selection. Meniscal repair has the
      benefit of tissue preservation in exchange for a more lengthy rehabilitation, which is
      less desirable for the in-season athlete. MAT is a sensible option for the athlete with
      minimal viable meniscal tissue remaining and joint line pain who wishes to maintain
      an active lifestyle. As the surgeon, one must help the athlete to make a well-
      informed decision: one that will benefit the athlete’s career as well as preserving the
      health of the athlete’s knee.

5	      Return to Play Guidelines after Cervical Spine Injuries in American Football Athletes:
6	                                      A Literature-based Review
7	
8	
9	     Peter R. Swiatek MD1
10	     Tejas Nandurkar MS2
11	     Joseph Maroon MD3
12	     Robert Cantu MD4
13	     Henry Feuer MD5
14	     Julian Bailes MD6
15	     Wellington Hsu MD7
16	
17	
18	         1. Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Northwestern University Feinberg School of
19	            Medicine, Chicago, IL
20	         2. Chicago Medical School at Rosalind and Franklin University of Medicine and
21	            Science, Chicago, IL
22	         3. Professor of Neurological Surgery, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine,
23	            Pittsburgh, PA
24	         4. Professor of Neurological Surgery, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston,
25	            MA
26	         5. Neurological Spine Surgery, University of Indiana Methodist Sports Medicine,
27	            Indianapolis, IN
28	         6. Bennett-Tarkington Chair, Department of Neurosurgery, Co-Director, NorthShore
29	            Neurological Institute, Chicago, IL
30	         7. Professor of Orthopaedic Surgery and Neurological Surgery, Northwestern University
31	            Feinberg School of Medicine, Chicago, IL
32	     Corresponding Author:
33	     Peter R. Swiatek, MD
34	     676 N. Saint Clair, Suite 1350
35	     Chicago, Illinois 60611
36	     Ph: 312-926-4444
37	     Fax: 312-926-4643
38	
39

41	Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
42	      The manuscript submitted does not contain information about medical device(s)/drug(s).
43	     No funds were received in support of this work.
44	     Relevant financial activities outside the submitted work: grants.
45	
46	
47	     MINI ABSTRACT
48	     We review clinical and case studies related to return to play (RTP) after cervical spine
49	     injuries in elite American football athletes and offer management guidelines. The decision for
50	     RTP requires an understanding of RTP time, risks of recurrence or re-injury, and individual
51	     characteristics, including position played and pathology on imaging.
52	     ABSTRACT
53	     Study Design: Literature-based review
54	     Objective: We sought to evaluate clinical and case studies related to return to play (RTP)
55	     after cervical spine injuries in elite American football athletes and to formulate guidelines to
56	     help health care practitioners manage these conditions.
57	     Summary of Background Data: American football athletes are at unique risk of cervical
58	     spine injury and appropriate case-by-case management of cervical spine injuries is necessary
59	     for these athletes. Despite this need, no standardized guidelines exist for RTP after cervical
60	     spine injury.
61	     Methods: Observational or case-based articles relating to RTP after cervical spine injury in
62	     American football athletes were curated from PubMed/EMBASE databases. Primary
63	     literature published before December 1, 2019 involving National Football League (NFL) or
64	     National College Athlete Association (NCAA) athletes met inclusion criteria.
65	     Results: The data acquisition process yielded 28 studies addressing cervical spine injuries
66	     and RTP in American football athletes. Stingers/burners were the most common injury and
67	     placed athletes at higher risk of a more severe re-injury. Transient quadriplegia, cervical
68	     stenosis, cervical disc herniation (CDH), and cervical fractures have a more significant
69	     impact on the long-term health and career longevity of the American football athlete. As
70	     such, the literature offers some guidance for management of these athletes, including average
71	     time for RTP in patients treated non-operatively, thresholds involving cervical stenosis, and
72	     postoperative recommendations after spinal decompression and/or fusion surgery.
73	     Conclusion: Elite American football athletes are at high risk for cervical spine injury due to
74	     the nature of their sport. The decision to allow these athletes to return to play should involve
75	     an understanding of the average RTP time, the potential risks of recurrence or re-injury, and
76	     individual characteristics such as position played and pathology on imaging.
77	     Key Words: return to play, cervical spine injury, NFL, NCAA, athlete, football, cervical
78	     stenosis, stingers, burners, transient quadriplegia, cervical fracture, ACDF, spinal fusion
79	     Level of Evidence: 3
80	
81	
82	
83	Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
84	      INTRODUCTION
85	             The incidence, management, and outcomes after cervical spine injuries are of major
86	     interest for athletes participating in American football. From 2000 to 2010, nearly 1,000 NFL
87	     athletes suffered a cervical spine injury, accounting for 45% of all their spinal injuries in that
88	     timespan.1 Additionally, collegiate football athletes suffered nearly 7500 cervical spine
89	     injuries from 2009 to 2014.2 There are a variety of diagnoses within this group with each type
90	     associated with a different degree of severity, disability, and ability to participate in practices
91	     and games. Given the significance of its impact on American football player participation and
92	     performance, health care professionals need to be aware of the available literature and
93	     opinions as it pertains to diagnosis, treatment, and proper management of these injuries.
94	             Despite the prevalence of these conditions, there do not exist any standardized
95	     consensus guidelines for return to play. Many of the pertinent treatises for treatment in this
96	     population are based upon expert opinion only. Given the variety and complexity of cervical
97	     spine injuries that can affect players, it is likely that an algorithm that incorporates general
98	     guiding principles, the best available evidence, and consensus opinion amongst experts may
99	     be most appropriate for treatment of these players. The purpose of this study is to propose a
100	     set of evidence-based guidelines for return to play after cervical spine injury in American
101	     football athletes based upon a comprehensive literature review.
102	     METHODS
103	             An initial search was conducted using the MEDLINE database (PubMed, U.S.
104	     National Institutes of Health, National Library of Medicine) and the EMBASE (Elsevier,
105	     Netherlands). Articles listed for publication by December 1, 2019 met the inclusion criteria.
106	     We used keywords to identify those sources aimed at discussing return to play after cervical
107	     spine injury in American football athletes. The Boolean logic query is as follows: ('cervical
108	     spine injury' OR 'brachial plexus' OR 'cervical injury' OR 'cervical injuries' OR 'cervical
109	     strain' OR 'cervical sprain' OR 'stinger' OR 'burner' OR 'cervical stenosis' OR 'cervical cord
110	     neuropraxia' OR 'transient quadriplegia' OR 'cervical disc herniation' OR 'spear tackle
111	     spine' OR 'cervical fracture' OR 'acdf' OR 'anterior cervical discectomy and fusion') AND
112	     ('NFL' OR 'National Football League' OR 'football') AND ('return to
113	     play' OR 'rtp' OR 'return to competition' OR 'return to contact' OR 'return-to-play').
114	             Manual searches using the above keywords were also performed to identify additional
115	     papers discussing RTP in American football athletes with cervical injuries (Figure 1). Only
116	     articles published in English were included. Two independent reviewers completed an initial
117	     screening based upon review or title and abstracts. The final set of articles for full-text review
118	     were determined based upon the following set of inclusion: (1) discusses American football
119	     athletes participating at the National Football League (NFL) or National Collegiate Athletic
120	     Association (NCAA) levels, (2) includes at least one type of cervical spine injury or
121	     condition, (3) provides a detailed discussion of RTP after cervical injury. Exclusion criteria
122	     included qualitative literature reviews and purely editorial-based or opinion articles.
123	     Publications with minimal or no discussion of RTP were excluded. Additionally, studies
124	     focusing on sports other that professional or collegiate football, such as rugby or high school
125	     sports, were excluded.
126	Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
127	      Patient and Public Involvement
128	            Individual patients were not directly involved in the completion of this work; instead,
129	     this work represents a review of previously published data. Research questions were
130	     formulated based upon the need for more appropriate and evidence-based guidelines for
131	     treatment of cervical spine injuries in American football athletes.
132	     RESULTS
133	             A total of 28 publications met the inclusion criteria for this study (Supplementary
134	     Table 1, http://links.lww.com/BRS/B708). The pertinent injuries discussed included
135	     strains/sprains (n=4 studies), stingers/burners (n=7 studies), stenosis (n=19 studies), disc
136	     herniation (n=14 studies), and fractures (n=6 studies).
137	             For strains/sprains (n=4 studies), these injuries comprised nearly 37% of all cervical
138	     spine injuries in NFL athletes1 from 2000 to 2010 and 55% of collegiate football players from
139	     2009 to 2014.2 Strains/sprains appear to be self-limited and have been associated with
140	     minimal time away from play. For NFL athletes, strains and sprains have been associated
141	     with 6 and 10 days mean loss of playing time, respectively.1 Similarly, more than 90% of
142	     collegiate football athletes suffering strains/sprains lost fewer than 7 days of play.2
143	              Stingers/burners (n=7 studies) were the most common cause of cervical spine injury
144	     in elite American football athletes, accounting for 46%1 and 65%2 of all cervical injuries in
145	     NFL and collegiate athletes, respectively. NFL athletes with stingers/burners with persistent
146	     symptoms experienced an average of 15 days of playing time missed1 and 97% of collegiate
147	     athletes with stingers/burners missed fewer than 21 days of playing time.2
148	             Transient quadriplegia (n=19 studies) occurred in 7.3 per 10,000 professional football
149	     players and is closely associated with the presence of congenital cervical stenosis, which puts
150	     the player at risk with extreme flexion and extension of the cervical spine 3-10. Historically,
151	     Torg et al suggested RTP recommendations for NFL athletes based upon 0.8 vertebral canal-
152	     to-body ratio on plain radiographs and presence of symptoms. However, in a CT-based
153	     evaluation of 80 NFL athletes, Herzog et al11 demonstrated that nearly 50% of asymptomatic
154	     players had abnormal canal-to-body ratios, despite having average spinal canal measurements
155	     on advanced imaging. These data challenge the specificity for the usage of this test in this
156	     patient population. More recent studies have identified the sagittal MRI as the most
157	     appropriate screening tool to diagnose cervical stenosis.12,13 For example, the term
158	     “congenital cervical stenosis” has recently been specifically defined as a patient less than 50
159	     years of age with mid-sagittal canal diameters of < 10 mm at multiple sub-axial cervical
160	     levels measured at the pedicle on MRI T2 imaging.14 Furthermore, Aebli et al recently
161	     reported that a sagittal canal diameter of less than 8 mm may increase the risk of spinal cord
162	     injury with minor trauma to the neck.15 MRI evaluation can also lead to the qualitative
163	     diagnosis of stenosis, or “functional cervical spinal stenosis,” that grades severity by the loss
164	     of protective cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) around the spinal cord.6
165	             Cervical disc herniations (CDH) (n=14 studies), from 2000 to 2010, accounted for
166	     5.8% of cervical spine injuries in NFL athletes resulting in an average of 85 days of lost
167	     practice and game activity.16 Proportionately fewer collegiate football players, approximately

170	      2%, suffered CDH from 2009 to 2014 and nearly 30% of these athletes lost more than 3
171	     weeks of play.2 From a position perspective, this injury has been most commonly reported in
172	     both linebackers and defensive backs, accounting for 18% and 16% of all CDH cases in NFL
173	     athletes, respectively. Furthermore, performance outcomes after surgical treatment may be
174	     worse for players of these positions than others.17 In general, after a single-level surgery for
175	     CDH, postoperative outcomes are favorable, with 72% successfully returning to play for an
176	     average of 29 games over a 2.8-years period, while only 46% of NFL players treated non-
177	     operatively successfully returned to play for an average of 15 games over a 1.5 years
178	     period.18,19 Maroon et al20 demonstrated in a smaller case series that 80% were able to return
179	     to play approximately nine months after ACDF.21
180	             While some experts have suggested that NFL and other American football players
181	     suffering CDH in the upper cervical spine (C2-4) should not return to collision sports after
182	     ACDF due to the catastrophic risk of adjacent segment disease in the upper cervical region,22
183	     Mai et al found no significant difference in RTP for NFL athletes treated surgical for upper
184	     (C2-4) versus lower (C4-T1) CDH.17 Because NFL athletes are more prone to developing
185	     upper cervical (C3-4) pathology compared to the general population,1,16,23,24 the decision-
186	     making process for these types of conditions are pertinent. Rates of adjacent segment disease
187	     in post-ACDF NFL athletes have been reported to be comparable to that of the general
188	     population.17,25 Finally, American football athletes who undergo surgical management of
189	     CDH with foraminotomy have a higher return-to-play rate and shorter recovery time, but are
190	     at higher risk of requiring re-operation.17,26
191	              A total of 18 cervical fractures (n=6 studies) were reported in the NFL between 2000-
192	          1
193	     2010 . According to Mall et al, cervical fractures were associated with a 120-day recovery
194	     period before RTP. Specific treatment of these injuries depends upon fracture pattern and
195	     stability,27 but with regard to collegiate football, Chung reported a total of 114 cervical spine
196	     fractures from 2009 to 2014 that were all treated non-operatively.2
197	     DISCUSSION
198	             The diagnosis, management, and decision-making process surrounding cervical spinal
199	     injuries in American football athletes can be complex and must incorporate many different
200	     considerations – both short- and long-term. Even though players have been treated for these
201	     conditions for over a century, only recently has some evidence-based literature emerged to
202	     help guide health care practitioners with this challenging clinical problem. We believe that
203	     large-scale retrospective cohort, case series, and even case report studies can be incorporated
204	     with expert opinion to set forth guidelines to practitioners and players who are afflicted by
205	     cervical spinal injuries.
206	     Cervical Strains and Sprains
207	             Many of the cervical spine injuries in NFL athletes involve the soft tissue supporting
208	     the cervical spine and may be classified as strains (muscular), or strains (ligamentous).
209	     Patients typically present with symptoms of neck pain with pain limiting range of motion and
210	     absence of distal numbness, tingling, or paresthesias. For these injuries, despite absence of a
211	     direct neurologic insult, medical evaluation is necessary to rule out cervical instability from
212	
213	Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
214	      ligamentous disruption or occult fractures. For example, although not necessarily a
215	     contraindication to RTP, discovery of a bipartite atlas has been reported on standard workup
216	     of a collegiate football player presenting with a sprain/strain.28 Guidelines for return to play
217	     after a cervical strain/sprain include pain-free full range-of-motion, normal strength, and the
218	     dearth of subluxation or abnormal curvature on cervical radiographs.9,29 Torg et al
219	     recommends that any NFL athletes who fail one of the aforementioned criteria should be
220	     protected in a cervical collar for 2 weeks and then evaluated with either flexion/extension
221	     radiographs or MRI to evaluate for intervertebral disc pathology if clinically warranted.9
222	     Stingers and Burners
223	             Stingers or burners are defined as a type of brachial plexopathy manifesting as
224	     transient sensory and/or motor deficits in the ipsilateral upper extremity resulting from
225	     compression- or traction-type trauma.30,31 Given the typical mechanisms of action, the upper
226	     and middle trunks arising from C5-C7 are more likely to be injured than C8-T1, which may
227	     be injured with forceful abduction and external rotation of the arm. 30 For athletes with
228	     recurrent injuries, cervical foraminal stenosis is commonly an associated pathology, as the
229	     dorsal root ganglion takes up the majority of space in the neural foramen and may be more
230	     susceptible to injury during a traumatic compression-type event.32 In our anecdotal
231	     experience, the incidence of recurrence is also increased when players are returned to full
232	     contact before complete resolution of symptoms.
233	             For these types of injuries, initial evaluation must rule out a more significant
234	     structural or spinal cord injury. For athletes with residual symptoms after injury such as
235	     limited ROM or neck pain, RTP should be postponed. After a first stinger with significant
236	     physical findings, evaluation should include cervical spine radiographs and MRI evaluation.
237	     CT and/or EMG (for chronic symptoms) can be considered in case-by-case instances. 29 In a
238	     modified Delphi consensus study that included 48 spine surgeons, of which 12 were either
239	     NCAA or NFL team physicians, Schroeder et al found that 84.5% of surgeons would allow
240	     RTP if symptoms lasted less than 5 minutes and would require additional evaluation for an
241	     episode lasting longer.33 With complete resolution of symptoms, guidelines for RTP after
242	     injury are the same as for a strain/sprain.
243	     Transient Quadriplegia and Cervical Stenosis
244	             Transient quadriplegia from a cervical cord concussion is defined as a temporary loss
245	     of motor or sensory function in the arms and legs that can last from seconds to days following
246	     excessive compression, flexion, or extension injury of the cervical spine. 3,34-37 The presence
247	     of pre-existing cervical stenosis greatly reduces functional reserve, which increases the
248	     incidence of these symptoms with hyperextension or axial compression forces.38 The severity
249	     of the episode also deserves consideration in the individualized return-to-play algorithm. The
250	     more severe and longer duration of symptoms, the greater ramifications and risk of
251	     neurologic sequelae with a repeat injury.
252	             There is a significant amount of controversy as it pertains to the diagnosis of cervical
253	     stenosis and the proper and safe return-to-play criteria39 for athletes of all sports. Based on
254	     the available literature to date, we believe that practitioners should rely upon four categories
255	
256	Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
257	      of information for the management of these conditions: clinical symptoms, physical
258	     examination, sport and position played, and imaging characteristics.40 In the setting of a
259	     player without any residual symptoms and normal strength and neurologic examination,
260	     individualized recommendations should rely upon the type of demands of the player’s
261	     respective sport as well as what the advanced imaging (e.g, MRI) studies demonstrate. The
262	     categorization of collision (i.e. American football, rugby, hockey, etc.) versus contact sports
263	     (basketball, soccer, lacrosse, etc.) is important because of the relative risk of repetitive and
264	     traumatic hyperextension and axial compression forces to the cervical spine. In our opinion,
265	     collision sports such as American football represent a significantly higher risk of re-injury in
266	     players with stenosis than contact sports.
267	             Based on the most recent literature, we believe that the measurement of the cervical
268	     spinal canal diameter on sagittal T2 MRI provides the most specific information in the
269	     diagnosis of this condition. Although historically cervical spinal stenosis has been defined as
270	     a space available for the cord < 14 mm on plain radiographs,41 more recent and pertinent data
271	     suggest that this threshold may be too conservative when it comes to the risk of a spinal cord
272	     injury in the American football population. The data from Schroeder et al suggests that 10-
273	     mm sagittal canal diameter is compatible with successful NFL careers without increased risk
274	     of neurologic sequelae despite a small sample size.42 Furthermore, Aebli et al demonstrated
275	     that sagittal canal diameter of < 8 mm on MRI increases the risk of acute spinal cord injury
276	     after minor trauma to the cervical spine.15 Although there are certainly other data that utilizes
277	     other measures of spinal canal space,43 most of the evidence-based literature points towards
278	     this range as a potential threshold for return-to-play criteria when treating these athletes. In a
279	     systematic review of clinical studies involving high-energy contact athletes, Dailey et al
280	     strongly recommended that those without stenosis can return to play and weakly recommend
281	     that those with stenosis not return to play after one episode of transient cervical cord
282	     neurapraxia.3
283	             In players with cervical stenosis, absolute contraindications of RTP4 include
284	     persistent neurological symptoms, cervical pain, loss of ROM, os odontoideum, basilar
285	     invagination, atlanto-occipital instability, Chiari malformation, functional spinal stenosis,
286	     cervical instability due to fracture or ligamentous disruption, symptoms lasting >36 hours, or
287	     repeat episodes of transient quadriplegia 4,34,44. RTP recommendations in NFL athletes who
288	     demonstrate persistent cord hyperintensity despite surgical treatment is controversial.45 While
289	     the presence of residual edema in the spinal cord may represent smaller reserve to withstand
290	     future forces on the cervical spine, Maroon et al recommends that cord hyperintensity after
291	     surgery may not preclude RTP in NFL athletes.12,20 Tempel et al also reported persistent T2
292	     hyperintensity in 3 professional athletes, all of whom returned to play without re-injury.12 In
293	     their modified Delphi analysis, Schroeder et al found strong consensus among physician
294	     regarding RTP in asymptomatic patients with no signal changes and canal diameter >10mm
295	     or resolved signal changes and canal diameter >13mm. Those with no history of signal
296	     changes and canal diameters <10mm should be considered on case-by-case basis and those
297	     with resolved signal changes and canal diameters <10mm should not RTP. No consensus was
298	     reached for patients with persistent signal changes.33

302	              In summary, RTP indications for patients with a history of congenital cervical
303	     stenosis or transient quadriplegia are controversial. Imaging studies should be considered in
304	     context with the athlete’s history, mechanism of injury, physical examination, and discussion
305	     of specific RTP risks with the athletes.13,46,47
306	     Cervical Disc Herniation
307	             CDH, which is a career-threatening injury, is more common in NFL and other contact
308	     athletes relative to the general population.1,48 The injury is associated with upper extremity
309	     radiculopathy, pain with range of motion, and/or coordination difficulties. Players without
310	     significant nerve root compression may be treated conservatively and return to play upon
311	     regaining full cervical motion and upper extremity strength.9,49
312	             Both non-operative and operative treatments of CDH have been proven to be
313	     successful, which indicates that players with this condition in the absence of neurologic
314	     deficits or myelopathy can heal without aggressive treatment. For example, in their review of
315	     16 NFL athletes with CDH, Meredith et al describes 8 players who were treated non-
316	     operatively with therapy, NSAIDs, or epidural steroid injections and successfully returned to
317	     play.49 Hsu et al reviewed 99 NFL athletes with CDH and found that although operative
318	     management was associated with higher RTP compared to non-operative management,
319	     performance scores and numbers of games started was not different between treatment
320	     groups.18 As with cases of CDH in non-football athletes, initial management of CDH should
321	     include a trial of non-operative management which could include epidural injections and anti-
322	     neuropathic agents.
323	             For patients with persistent pain, significant extremity weakness, or cervical stenosis
324	     are present, operative management has demonstrated successful RTP. While anterior cervical
325	     discectomy and fusion is the most common operation offered to these players, posterior
326	     foraminotomies can also be successful for appropriate pathology. Recent data suggest that
327	     players who undergo a foraminotomy need to be counseled as to the significant increased risk
328	     of reoperation compared to a fusion, but depending on the goals of the player and medical
329	     team, this can be a reasonable option. An athlete who has undergone a single-level anterior or
330	     posterior fusion who is asymptomatic, neurologically intact, without pain or ROM restriction,
331	     and evidence of radiographic fusion, can be cleared to return to sport;49 however, the athlete
332	     may be at increased risk of repeated herniation above or below the fused level.50 This
333	     recommendation is supported by Schroeder et al in their Delphi analysis. However, when
334	     considering asymptomatic players without symptoms, no T2-signal changes, and solid 2-level
335	     ACDF fusions, the authors found no consensus among team physicians regarding RTP.33
336	     Similarly, they found only weak consensus among experts regarding the case-by-case
337	     consideration needed for athletes undergoing corpectomy or posterior cervical surgery.33
338	             Relative contraindications to RTP include athletes with an asymptomatic
339	     pseudarthrosis, 2- and 3-level fusion, and/or persistent signal intensity of T2 imaging.9
340	     Absolute contraindications to RTP include persistent neurologic findings, ROM limitations,
341	     pain, 4+ level anterior or posterior fusions.9

346	      Cervical Fractures
347	              Cervical fractures can occur when the area between the vertebral body and
348	     decelerating head undergoes rapid compression, requiring as little as 150ft lbs of force to
349	     fracture the cervical vertebrae.29,51,52 Certain fracture patterns involving the spinous process
350	     or unilateral lamina do not typically cause significant instability and require only hard collar
351	     immobilization for a period of 6-12 weeks as definitive treatment. 44 Stability on flexion-
352	     extension radiographs after healing and maintenance of cervical lordosis are required for
353	     RTP.29,51 Unstable fractures are best treated with surgical fixation,27,29,47 and in general, the
354	     literature supports return to play for players who are treated with a one-level subaxial anterior
355	     or posterior fusion if there is no pain, full ROM, normal muscle strength, complete fusion on
356	     imaging, and a normal neurological exam.13
357	             The decision to allow an athlete to RTP is highly dependent upon surgeon and pattern
358	     of injury. For example, in their case-based survey study, France et al found that 12% of spine
359	     surgeons would not allow a collegiate football player with a non-operatively healed C5 burst
360	     fracture to return to football.39 In their case-based questionnaire of 113 sports and spine
361	     physicians, Morganti et al. found similar disagreement in management of certain subaxial
362	     cervical spine injuries treated with one-level fusion.8 Schroeder et al found that unanimous
363	     consensus among an expert panel of spine surgeons regarding RTP in athletes with solid
364	     fusion after burst, compression, or facet fracture with no instability, no T2 signal change, and
365	     solid fusion.33
366	             Despite some disagreements, there appears to be strong consensus regarding certain
367	     absolute contraindications, including any patient with a fracture with residual neurological
368	     deficits, underlying congenital stenosis, cervical laminectomy, and any procedures that
369	     require occipital, C1-C2, C2-C3, or 3+ level fusions.29,53,54 Consideration for NFL athlete
370	     RTP should involve imaging demonstrating solid fusion in the area of injury, lack of
371	     instability on flexion and extension radiographs, maintenance of normal cervical lordosis, full
372	     ROM with no associated pain, and preinjury muscle strength. 29,44,53 Additionally, sagittal
373	     misalignment >11° when compared to other levels for isolated burst fractures and fractures
374	     that disrupt the posterior bony or ligamentous tension band may preclude RTP. 44,53
375	             Our ability to develop generalizable recommendations for RTP in American football
376	     athletes after cervical spine injury is with substantial limitation. The majority of primary
377	     sources used for developing RTP recommendations were cases studies, panel discussions, or
378	     review of general injury data that is limited by lack of clinical granularity. Although certain
379	     recommendations are strongly supported by the literature (athletes with persistent
380	     neurological symptoms should not RTP), others are less robust or even controversial. In these
381	     cases, individual surgeons must rely upon experience and patient-specific factors for making
382	     RTP decisions. Given the lack of high-level evidence directing RTP after cervical spine
383	     injury, there is a theoretical risk that this consensus-based approach to managing cervical
384	     spine injuries may become more dogma than guideline. However, we acknowledge that the
385	     purpose of this review is to generate guiding principles rather than rules for the management
386	     of cervical spine injuries in athletes and to encourage future reseach efforts aimed at
387	     improving the evidence for RTP.

390	              The development of strong recommendations for RTP and cervical spine injuries in
391	     football athletes requires a strong study design, prospective collection, and outcomes data
392	     both on and off the field. Major professional sport organizations all have this mechanism in
393	     place, however, the approach and type of allowable data to be collected varies widely55. We
394	     believe that if medical staff of professional sports are allowed to prospectively collect data on
395	     spine injuries in athletes and assess post-treatment outcomes through patient-reported
396	     outcomes and statistical performance then the controversial questions in this population that
397	     spine physicians struggle with can be answered. While some major North American sport
398	     leagues currently allow for this, many critical ones do not.
399	     Conclusion
400	             Although an improved understanding of injury mechanisms as well as the evolution of
401	     rule changes have decreased its incidence, cervical spine injuries continue to occur frequently
402	     in American football. These conditions present a myriad of challenges and can result in
403	     significant consequences for players with improper management. RTP guidelines after injury
404	     need to be assessed based on a case-by-case basis, but we believe in several core principles.
405	     Consideration for RTP should be individualized based upon a player’s history, physical
406	     examination, imaging characteristics, and sport/position played. Players should have full
407	     ROM of the cervical spine without associated pain, return of normal muscle strength, and an
408	     intact neurologic exam. Recommendations regarding congenital issues in the cervical spine
409	     and postsurgical criteria for RTP continue to evolve with the continued research of cervical
410	     spine injuries in NFL athletes.

413	     KEY POINTS
414	            Elite American football athletes are a unique patient population who are at increased
415	             risk for cervical spine injury.
416	            This study proposes a set of evidence-based guidelines for return to play after cervical
417	             spine injury in American football athletes.
418	            These guidelines incorporate general guiding principles, best available evidence, and
419	             consensus opinion among experts.
420	            This review and consensus work will guide spine surgeons and sports practitioners in
421	             the management of American football athletes with cervical spine injuries.

      Return to Play Guidelines after Cervical Spine Injuries in American Football Athletes:
                                      A Literature-based Review


     Peter R. Swiatek MD1
     Tejas Nandurkar MS2
     Joseph Maroon MD3
     Robert Cantu MD4
     Henry Feuer MD5
     Julian Bailes MD6
     Wellington Hsu MD7


         1. Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Northwestern University Feinberg School of
            Medicine, Chicago, IL
         2. Chicago Medical School at Rosalind and Franklin University of Medicine and
            Science, Chicago, IL
         3. Professor of Neurological Surgery, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine,
            Pittsburgh, PA
         4. Professor of Neurological Surgery, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston,
            MA
         5. Neurological Spine Surgery, University of Indiana Methodist Sports Medicine,
            Indianapolis, IN
         6. Bennett-Tarkington Chair, Department of Neurosurgery, Co-Director, NorthShore
            Neurological Institute, Chicago, IL
         7. Professor of Orthopaedic Surgery and Neurological Surgery, Northwestern University
            Feinberg School of Medicine, Chicago, IL
     Corresponding Author:
     Peter R. Swiatek, MD
     676 N. Saint Clair, Suite 1350
     Chicago, Illinois 60611
     Ph: 312-926-4444
     Fax: 312-926-4643

     MINI ABSTRACT
     We review clinical and case studies related to return to play (RTP) after cervical spine
     injuries in elite American football athletes and offer management guidelines. The decision for
     RTP requires an understanding of RTP time, risks of recurrence or re-injury, and individual
     characteristics, including position played and pathology on imaging.
     ABSTRACT
     Study Design: Literature-based review
     Objective: We sought to evaluate clinical and case studies related to return to play (RTP)
     after cervical spine injuries in elite American football athletes and to formulate guidelines to
     help health care practitioners manage these conditions.
     Summary of Background Data: American football athletes are at unique risk of cervical
     spine injury and appropriate case-by-case management of cervical spine injuries is necessary
     for these athletes. Despite this need, no standardized guidelines exist for RTP after cervical
     spine injury.
     Methods: Observational or case-based articles relating to RTP after cervical spine injury in
     American football athletes were curated from PubMed/EMBASE databases. Primary
     literature published before December 1, 2019 involving National Football League (NFL) or
     National College Athlete Association (NCAA) athletes met inclusion criteria.
     Results: The data acquisition process yielded 28 studies addressing cervical spine injuries
     and RTP in American football athletes. Stingers/burners were the most common injury and
     placed athletes at higher risk of a more severe re-injury. Transient quadriplegia, cervical
     stenosis, cervical disc herniation (CDH), and cervical fractures have a more significant
     impact on the long-term health and career longevity of the American football athlete. As
     such, the literature offers some guidance for management of these athletes, including average
     time for RTP in patients treated non-operatively, thresholds involving cervical stenosis, and
     postoperative recommendations after spinal decompression and/or fusion surgery.
     Conclusion: Elite American football athletes are at high risk for cervical spine injury due to
     the nature of their sport. The decision to allow these athletes to return to play should involve
     an understanding of the average RTP time, the potential risks of recurrence or re-injury, and
     individual characteristics such as position played and pathology on imaging.
     Key Words: return to play, cervical spine injury, NFL, NCAA, athlete, football, cervical
     stenosis, stingers, burners, transient quadriplegia, cervical fracture, ACDF, spinal fusion
     Level of Evidence: 3



Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
      INTRODUCTION
             The incidence, management, and outcomes after cervical spine injuries are of major
     interest for athletes participating in American football. From 2000 to 2010, nearly 1,000 NFL
     athletes suffered a cervical spine injury, accounting for 45% of all their spinal injuries in that
     timespan.1 Additionally, collegiate football athletes suffered nearly 7500 cervical spine
     injuries from 2009 to 2014.2 There are a variety of diagnoses within this group with each type
     associated with a different degree of severity, disability, and ability to participate in practices
     and games. Given the significance of its impact on American football player participation and
     performance, health care professionals need to be aware of the available literature and
     opinions as it pertains to diagnosis, treatment, and proper management of these injuries.
             Despite the prevalence of these conditions, there do not exist any standardized
     consensus guidelines for return to play. Many of the pertinent treatises for treatment in this
     population are based upon expert opinion only. Given the variety and complexity of cervical
     spine injuries that can affect players, it is likely that an algorithm that incorporates general
     guiding principles, the best available evidence, and consensus opinion amongst experts may
     be most appropriate for treatment of these players. The purpose of this study is to propose a
     set of evidence-based guidelines for return to play after cervical spine injury in American
     football athletes based upon a comprehensive literature review.
     METHODS
             An initial search was conducted using the MEDLINE database (PubMed, U.S.
     National Institutes of Health, National Library of Medicine) and the EMBASE (Elsevier,
     Netherlands). Articles listed for publication by December 1, 2019 met the inclusion criteria.
     We used keywords to identify those sources aimed at discussing return to play after cervical
     spine injury in American football athletes. The Boolean logic query is as follows: ('cervical
     spine injury' OR 'brachial plexus' OR 'cervical injury' OR 'cervical injuries' OR 'cervical
     strain' OR 'cervical sprain' OR 'stinger' OR 'burner' OR 'cervical stenosis' OR 'cervical cord
     neuropraxia' OR 'transient quadriplegia' OR 'cervical disc herniation' OR 'spear tackle
     spine' OR 'cervical fracture' OR 'acdf' OR 'anterior cervical discectomy and fusion') AND
     ('NFL' OR 'National Football League' OR 'football') AND ('return to
     play' OR 'rtp' OR 'return to competition' OR 'return to contact' OR 'return-to-play').
             Manual searches using the above keywords were also performed to identify additional
     papers discussing RTP in American football athletes with cervical injuries (Figure 1). Only
     articles published in English were included. Two independent reviewers completed an initial
     screening based upon review or title and abstracts. The final set of articles for full-text review
     were determined based upon the following set of inclusion: (1) discusses American football
     athletes participating at the National Football League (NFL) or National Collegiate Athletic
     Association (NCAA) levels, (2) includes at least one type of cervical spine injury or
     condition, (3) provides a detailed discussion of RTP after cervical injury. Exclusion criteria
     included qualitative literature reviews and purely editorial-based or opinion articles.
     Publications with minimal or no discussion of RTP were excluded. Additionally, studies
     focusing on sports other that professional or collegiate football, such as rugby or high school
     sports, were excluded.
Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
      Patient and Public Involvement
            Individual patients were not directly involved in the completion of this work; instead,
     this work represents a review of previously published data. Research questions were
     formulated based upon the need for more appropriate and evidence-based guidelines for
     treatment of cervical spine injuries in American football athletes.
     RESULTS
             A total of 28 publications met the inclusion criteria for this study (Supplementary
     Table 1, http://links.lww.com/BRS/B708). The pertinent injuries discussed included
     strains/sprains (n=4 studies), stingers/burners (n=7 studies), stenosis (n=19 studies), disc
     herniation (n=14 studies), and fractures (n=6 studies).
             For strains/sprains (n=4 studies), these injuries comprised nearly 37% of all cervical
     spine injuries in NFL athletes1 from 2000 to 2010 and 55% of collegiate football players from
     2009 to 2014.2 Strains/sprains appear to be self-limited and have been associated with
     minimal time away from play. For NFL athletes, strains and sprains have been associated
     with 6 and 10 days mean loss of playing time, respectively.1 Similarly, more than 90% of
     collegiate football athletes suffering strains/sprains lost fewer than 7 days of play.2
              Stingers/burners (n=7 studies) were the most common cause of cervical spine injury
     in elite American football athletes, accounting for 46%1 and 65%2 of all cervical injuries in
     NFL and collegiate athletes, respectively. NFL athletes with stingers/burners with persistent
     symptoms experienced an average of 15 days of playing time missed1 and 97% of collegiate
     athletes with stingers/burners missed fewer than 21 days of playing time.2
             Transient quadriplegia (n=19 studies) occurred in 7.3 per 10,000 professional football
     players and is closely associated with the presence of congenital cervical stenosis, which puts
     the player at risk with extreme flexion and extension of the cervical spine 3-10. Historically,
     Torg et al suggested RTP recommendations for NFL athletes based upon 0.8 vertebral canal-
     to-body ratio on plain radiographs and presence of symptoms. However, in a CT-based
     evaluation of 80 NFL athletes, Herzog et al11 demonstrated that nearly 50% of asymptomatic
     players had abnormal canal-to-body ratios, despite having average spinal canal measurements
     on advanced imaging. These data challenge the specificity for the usage of this test in this
     patient population. More recent studies have identified the sagittal MRI as the most
     appropriate screening tool to diagnose cervical stenosis.12,13 For example, the term
     “congenital cervical stenosis” has recently been specifically defined as a patient less than 50
     years of age with mid-sagittal canal diameters of < 10 mm at multiple sub-axial cervical
     levels measured at the pedicle on MRI T2 imaging.14 Furthermore, Aebli et al recently
     reported that a sagittal canal diameter of less than 8 mm may increase the risk of spinal cord
     injury with minor trauma to the neck.15 MRI evaluation can also lead to the qualitative
     diagnosis of stenosis, or “functional cervical spinal stenosis,” that grades severity by the loss
     of protective cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) around the spinal cord.6
             Cervical disc herniations (CDH) (n=14 studies), from 2000 to 2010, accounted for
     5.8% of cervical spine injuries in NFL athletes resulting in an average of 85 days of lost
     practice and game activity.16 Proportionately fewer collegiate football players, approximately

Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
      2%, suffered CDH from 2009 to 2014 and nearly 30% of these athletes lost more than 3
     weeks of play.2 From a position perspective, this injury has been most commonly reported in
     both linebackers and defensive backs, accounting for 18% and 16% of all CDH cases in NFL
     athletes, respectively. Furthermore, performance outcomes after surgical treatment may be
     worse for players of these positions than others.17 In general, after a single-level surgery for
     CDH, postoperative outcomes are favorable, with 72% successfully returning to play for an
     average of 29 games over a 2.8-years period, while only 46% of NFL players treated non-
     operatively successfully returned to play for an average of 15 games over a 1.5 years
     period.18,19 Maroon et al20 demonstrated in a smaller case series that 80% were able to return
     to play approximately nine months after ACDF.21
             While some experts have suggested that NFL and other American football players
     suffering CDH in the upper cervical spine (C2-4) should not return to collision sports after
     ACDF due to the catastrophic risk of adjacent segment disease in the upper cervical region,22
     Mai et al found no significant difference in RTP for NFL athletes treated surgical for upper
     (C2-4) versus lower (C4-T1) CDH.17 Because NFL athletes are more prone to developing
     upper cervical (C3-4) pathology compared to the general population,1,16,23,24 the decision-
     making process for these types of conditions are pertinent. Rates of adjacent segment disease
     in post-ACDF NFL athletes have been reported to be comparable to that of the general
     population.17,25 Finally, American football athletes who undergo surgical management of
     CDH with foraminotomy have a higher return-to-play rate and shorter recovery time, but are
     at higher risk of requiring re-operation.17,26
              A total of 18 cervical fractures (n=6 studies) were reported in the NFL between 2000-
          1
     2010 . According to Mall et al, cervical fractures were associated with a 120-day recovery
     period before RTP. Specific treatment of these injuries depends upon fracture pattern and
     stability,27 but with regard to collegiate football, Chung reported a total of 114 cervical spine
     fractures from 2009 to 2014 that were all treated non-operatively.2
     DISCUSSION
             The diagnosis, management, and decision-making process surrounding cervical spinal
     injuries in American football athletes can be complex and must incorporate many different
     considerations – both short- and long-term. Even though players have been treated for these
     conditions for over a century, only recently has some evidence-based literature emerged to
     help guide health care practitioners with this challenging clinical problem. We believe that
     large-scale retrospective cohort, case series, and even case report studies can be incorporated
     with expert opinion to set forth guidelines to practitioners and players who are afflicted by
     cervical spinal injuries.
     Cervical Strains and Sprains
             Many of the cervical spine injuries in NFL athletes involve the soft tissue supporting
     the cervical spine and may be classified as strains (muscular), or strains (ligamentous).
     Patients typically present with symptoms of neck pain with pain limiting range of motion and
     absence of distal numbness, tingling, or paresthesias. For these injuries, despite absence of a
     direct neurologic insult, medical evaluation is necessary to rule out cervical instability from

Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
      ligamentous disruption or occult fractures. For example, although not necessarily a
     contraindication to RTP, discovery of a bipartite atlas has been reported on standard workup
     of a collegiate football player presenting with a sprain/strain.28 Guidelines for return to play
     after a cervical strain/sprain include pain-free full range-of-motion, normal strength, and the
     dearth of subluxation or abnormal curvature on cervical radiographs.9,29 Torg et al
     recommends that any NFL athletes who fail one of the aforementioned criteria should be
     protected in a cervical collar for 2 weeks and then evaluated with either flexion/extension
     radiographs or MRI to evaluate for intervertebral disc pathology if clinically warranted.9
     Stingers and Burners
             Stingers or burners are defined as a type of brachial plexopathy manifesting as
     transient sensory and/or motor deficits in the ipsilateral upper extremity resulting from
     compression- or traction-type trauma.30,31 Given the typical mechanisms of action, the upper
     and middle trunks arising from C5-C7 are more likely to be injured than C8-T1, which may
     be injured with forceful abduction and external rotation of the arm. 30 For athletes with
     recurrent injuries, cervical foraminal stenosis is commonly an associated pathology, as the
     dorsal root ganglion takes up the majority of space in the neural foramen and may be more
     susceptible to injury during a traumatic compression-type event.32 In our anecdotal
     experience, the incidence of recurrence is also increased when players are returned to full
     contact before complete resolution of symptoms.
             For these types of injuries, initial evaluation must rule out a more significant
     structural or spinal cord injury. For athletes with residual symptoms after injury such as
     limited ROM or neck pain, RTP should be postponed. After a first stinger with significant
     physical findings, evaluation should include cervical spine radiographs and MRI evaluation.
     CT and/or EMG (for chronic symptoms) can be considered in case-by-case instances. 29 In a
     modified Delphi consensus study that included 48 spine surgeons, of which 12 were either
     NCAA or NFL team physicians, Schroeder et al found that 84.5% of surgeons would allow
     RTP if symptoms lasted less than 5 minutes and would require additional evaluation for an
     episode lasting longer.33 With complete resolution of symptoms, guidelines for RTP after
     injury are the same as for a strain/sprain.
     Transient Quadriplegia and Cervical Stenosis
             Transient quadriplegia from a cervical cord concussion is defined as a temporary loss
     of motor or sensory function in the arms and legs that can last from seconds to days following
     excessive compression, flexion, or extension injury of the cervical spine. 3,34-37 The presence
     of pre-existing cervical stenosis greatly reduces functional reserve, which increases the
     incidence of these symptoms with hyperextension or axial compression forces.38 The severity
     of the episode also deserves consideration in the individualized return-to-play algorithm. The
     more severe and longer duration of symptoms, the greater ramifications and risk of
     neurologic sequelae with a repeat injury.
             There is a significant amount of controversy as it pertains to the diagnosis of cervical
     stenosis and the proper and safe return-to-play criteria39 for athletes of all sports. Based on
     the available literature to date, we believe that practitioners should rely upon four categories

Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
      of information for the management of these conditions: clinical symptoms, physical
     examination, sport and position played, and imaging characteristics.40 In the setting of a
     player without any residual symptoms and normal strength and neurologic examination,
     individualized recommendations should rely upon the type of demands of the player’s
     respective sport as well as what the advanced imaging (e.g, MRI) studies demonstrate. The
     categorization of collision (i.e. American football, rugby, hockey, etc.) versus contact sports
     (basketball, soccer, lacrosse, etc.) is important because of the relative risk of repetitive and
     traumatic hyperextension and axial compression forces to the cervical spine. In our opinion,
     collision sports such as American football represent a significantly higher risk of re-injury in
     players with stenosis than contact sports.
             Based on the most recent literature, we believe that the measurement of the cervical
     spinal canal diameter on sagittal T2 MRI provides the most specific information in the
     diagnosis of this condition. Although historically cervical spinal stenosis has been defined as
     a space available for the cord < 14 mm on plain radiographs,41 more recent and pertinent data
     suggest that this threshold may be too conservative when it comes to the risk of a spinal cord
     injury in the American football population. The data from Schroeder et al suggests that 10-
     mm sagittal canal diameter is compatible with successful NFL careers without increased risk
     of neurologic sequelae despite a small sample size.42 Furthermore, Aebli et al demonstrated
     that sagittal canal diameter of < 8 mm on MRI increases the risk of acute spinal cord injury
     after minor trauma to the cervical spine.15 Although there are certainly other data that utilizes
     other measures of spinal canal space,43 most of the evidence-based literature points towards
     this range as a potential threshold for return-to-play criteria when treating these athletes. In a
     systematic review of clinical studies involving high-energy contact athletes, Dailey et al
     strongly recommended that those without stenosis can return to play and weakly recommend
     that those with stenosis not return to play after one episode of transient cervical cord
     neurapraxia.3
             In players with cervical stenosis, absolute contraindications of RTP4 include
     persistent neurological symptoms, cervical pain, loss of ROM, os odontoideum, basilar
     invagination, atlanto-occipital instability, Chiari malformation, functional spinal stenosis,
     cervical instability due to fracture or ligamentous disruption, symptoms lasting >36 hours, or
     repeat episodes of transient quadriplegia 4,34,44. RTP recommendations in NFL athletes who
     demonstrate persistent cord hyperintensity despite surgical treatment is controversial.45 While
     the presence of residual edema in the spinal cord may represent smaller reserve to withstand
     future forces on the cervical spine, Maroon et al recommends that cord hyperintensity after
     surgery may not preclude RTP in NFL athletes.12,20 Tempel et al also reported persistent T2
     hyperintensity in 3 professional athletes, all of whom returned to play without re-injury.12 In
     their modified Delphi analysis, Schroeder et al found strong consensus among physician
     regarding RTP in asymptomatic patients with no signal changes and canal diameter >10mm
     or resolved signal changes and canal diameter >13mm. Those with no history of signal
     changes and canal diameters <10mm should be considered on case-by-case basis and those
     with resolved signal changes and canal diameters <10mm should not RTP. No consensus was
     reached for patients with persistent signal changes.33


Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
              In summary, RTP indications for patients with a history of congenital cervical
     stenosis or transient quadriplegia are controversial. Imaging studies should be considered in
     context with the athlete’s history, mechanism of injury, physical examination, and discussion
     of specific RTP risks with the athletes.13,46,47
     Cervical Disc Herniation
             CDH, which is a career-threatening injury, is more common in NFL and other contact
     athletes relative to the general population.1,48 The injury is associated with upper extremity
     radiculopathy, pain with range of motion, and/or coordination difficulties. Players without
     significant nerve root compression may be treated conservatively and return to play upon
     regaining full cervical motion and upper extremity strength.9,49
             Both non-operative and operative treatments of CDH have been proven to be
     successful, which indicates that players with this condition in the absence of neurologic
     deficits or myelopathy can heal without aggressive treatment. For example, in their review of
     16 NFL athletes with CDH, Meredith et al describes 8 players who were treated non-
     operatively with therapy, NSAIDs, or epidural steroid injections and successfully returned to
     play.49 Hsu et al reviewed 99 NFL athletes with CDH and found that although operative
     management was associated with higher RTP compared to non-operative management,
     performance scores and numbers of games started was not different between treatment
     groups.18 As with cases of CDH in non-football athletes, initial management of CDH should
     include a trial of non-operative management which could include epidural injections and anti-
     neuropathic agents.
             For patients with persistent pain, significant extremity weakness, or cervical stenosis
     are present, operative management has demonstrated successful RTP. While anterior cervical
     discectomy and fusion is the most common operation offered to these players, posterior
     foraminotomies can also be successful for appropriate pathology. Recent data suggest that
     players who undergo a foraminotomy need to be counseled as to the significant increased risk
     of reoperation compared to a fusion, but depending on the goals of the player and medical
     team, this can be a reasonable option. An athlete who has undergone a single-level anterior or
     posterior fusion who is asymptomatic, neurologically intact, without pain or ROM restriction,
     and evidence of radiographic fusion, can be cleared to return to sport;49 however, the athlete
     may be at increased risk of repeated herniation above or below the fused level.50 This
     recommendation is supported by Schroeder et al in their Delphi analysis. However, when
     considering asymptomatic players without symptoms, no T2-signal changes, and solid 2-level
     ACDF fusions, the authors found no consensus among team physicians regarding RTP.33
     Similarly, they found only weak consensus among experts regarding the case-by-case
     consideration needed for athletes undergoing corpectomy or posterior cervical surgery.33
             Relative contraindications to RTP include athletes with an asymptomatic
     pseudarthrosis, 2- and 3-level fusion, and/or persistent signal intensity of T2 imaging.9
     Absolute contraindications to RTP include persistent neurologic findings, ROM limitations,
     pain, 4+ level anterior or posterior fusions.9



Copyright © 2021 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
      Cervical Fractures
              Cervical fractures can occur when the area between the vertebral body and
     decelerating head undergoes rapid compression, requiring as little as 150ft lbs of force to
     fracture the cervical vertebrae.29,51,52 Certain fracture patterns involving the spinous process
     or unilateral lamina do not typically cause significant instability and require only hard collar
     immobilization for a period of 6-12 weeks as definitive treatment. 44 Stability on flexion-
     extension radiographs after healing and maintenance of cervical lordosis are required for
     RTP.29,51 Unstable fractures are best treated with surgical fixation,27,29,47 and in general, the
     literature supports return to play for players who are treated with a one-level subaxial anterior
     or posterior fusion if there is no pain, full ROM, normal muscle strength, complete fusion on
     imaging, and a normal neurological exam.13
             The decision to allow an athlete to RTP is highly dependent upon surgeon and pattern
     of injury. For example, in their case-based survey study, France et al found that 12% of spine
     surgeons would not allow a collegiate football player with a non-operatively healed C5 burst
     fracture to return to football.39 In their case-based questionnaire of 113 sports and spine
     physicians, Morganti et al. found similar disagreement in management of certain subaxial
     cervical spine injuries treated with one-level fusion.8 Schroeder et al found that unanimous
     consensus among an expert panel of spine surgeons regarding RTP in athletes with solid
     fusion after burst, compression, or facet fracture with no instability, no T2 signal change, and
     solid fusion.33
             Despite some disagreements, there appears to be strong consensus regarding certain
     absolute contraindications, including any patient with a fracture with residual neurological
     deficits, underlying congenital stenosis, cervical laminectomy, and any procedures that
     require occipital, C1-C2, C2-C3, or 3+ level fusions.29,53,54 Consideration for NFL athlete
     RTP should involve imaging demonstrating solid fusion in the area of injury, lack of
     instability on flexion and extension radiographs, maintenance of normal cervical lordosis, full
     ROM with no associated pain, and preinjury muscle strength. 29,44,53 Additionally, sagittal
     misalignment >11° when compared to other levels for isolated burst fractures and fractures
     that disrupt the posterior bony or ligamentous tension band may preclude RTP. 44,53
             Our ability to develop generalizable recommendations for RTP in American football
     athletes after cervical spine injury is with substantial limitation. The majority of primary
     sources used for developing RTP recommendations were cases studies, panel discussions, or
     review of general injury data that is limited by lack of clinical granularity. Although certain
     recommendations are strongly supported by the literature (athletes with persistent
     neurological symptoms should not RTP), others are less robust or even controversial. In these
     cases, individual surgeons must rely upon experience and patient-specific factors for making
     RTP decisions. Given the lack of high-level evidence directing RTP after cervical spine
     injury, there is a theoretical risk that this consensus-based approach to managing cervical
     spine injuries may become more dogma than guideline. However, we acknowledge that the
     purpose of this review is to generate guiding principles rather than rules for the management
     of cervical spine injuries in athletes and to encourage future reseach efforts aimed at
     improving the evidence for RTP.

              The development of strong recommendations for RTP and cervical spine injuries in
     football athletes requires a strong study design, prospective collection, and outcomes data
     both on and off the field. Major professional sport organizations all have this mechanism in
     place, however, the approach and type of allowable data to be collected varies widely55. We
     believe that if medical staff of professional sports are allowed to prospectively collect data on
     spine injuries in athletes and assess post-treatment outcomes through patient-reported
     outcomes and statistical performance then the controversial questions in this population that
     spine physicians struggle with can be answered. While some major North American sport
     leagues currently allow for this, many critical ones do not.
     Conclusion
             Although an improved understanding of injury mechanisms as well as the evolution of
     rule changes have decreased its incidence, cervical spine injuries continue to occur frequently
     in American football. These conditions present a myriad of challenges and can result in
     significant consequences for players with improper management. RTP guidelines after injury
     need to be assessed based on a case-by-case basis, but we believe in several core principles.
     Consideration for RTP should be individualized based upon a player’s history, physical
     examination, imaging characteristics, and sport/position played. Players should have full
     ROM of the cervical spine without associated pain, return of normal muscle strength, and an
     intact neurologic exam. Recommendations regarding congenital issues in the cervical spine
     and postsurgical criteria for RTP continue to evolve with the continued research of cervical
     spine injuries in NFL athletes.


     KEY POINTS
            Elite American football athletes are a unique patient population who are at increased
             risk for cervical spine injury.
            This study proposes a set of evidence-based guidelines for return to play after cervical
             spine injury in American football athletes.
            These guidelines incorporate general guiding principles, best available evidence, and
             consensus opinion among experts.
            This review and consensus work will guide spine surgeons and sports practitioners in
             the management of American football athletes with cervical spine injuries.

   "practicalImplications":"Decide return to play on the combined picture of symptoms, neurological and range-of-motion examination, position, sport demands and MRI findings rather than a single test. Players with persistent neurological symptoms, neck pain or range-of-motion loss should not return. After a first stinger with significant physical findings, imaging is advised, and return to full contact should wait for symptoms to resolve.",
   "athleteDev":"Use the return-to-play criteria to gate the return to full contact: pain-free full cervical range, normal strength and an intact neurological exam. The authors' anecdotal experience is that recurrence rises when players return to full contact before symptoms fully resolve, so build contact back in stages after a stinger.",
   "rtp":"The review gives return-to-play information for strains, stingers, disc herniation after surgery, fractures and stenosis, but most of it is expert opinion. It cannot set a validated clearance standard for any single diagnosis. It must not be used to clear a player with persistent neurological symptoms, which the authors list as an absolute contraindication."
 }

6	                          Return to play in professional football players following
7	                          traumatic cervical spine injury: expert opinions from the
8	                          National Football League spine surgeons
9	                          Presented at the 2024 AANS/CNS Joint Section on Disorders of the Spine and Peripheral Nerves
10	
11	                          *Michael D. White, MD,1 Andrew M. Hersh, MD,2 Carly Weber-Levine, MS,2 Kelly Jiang, MS,2
12	                          A. Daniel Davidar, MBBS,2 Victoria Bergstein, BA,2 Vikas N. Vattipally, BS,2
13	                          Scott L. Zuckerman, MD, MPH,3 Allen K. Sills, MD,3 Randall W. Porter, MD,1
14	                          and Nicholas Theodore, MD2
15	                          Department of Neurosurgery, Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, Arizona; 2Department of Neurosurgery, Johns Hopkins
16	                          1
17	
18	                          University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland; and 3Department of Neurological Surgery, Vanderbilt University Medical
19	                          Center, Nashville, Tennessee
20	
21	                          OBJECTIVE There is a paucity of high-quality return-to-play (RTP) data following treatment of cervical spine injuries
22	                          in contact sports. In this study, the authors gathered insights from National Football League (NFL) team spine surgeon
23	                          consultants to highlight current practices in treating cervical spine injuries and report decision-making regarding RTP in
24	                          professional American football players.
25	                          METHODS A cross-sectional, online survey was distributed to all NFL consulting physicians specializing in the manage-
26	                          ment of spine injuries. The survey covered the following five clinical vignettes of cervical spine injuries: 1) radiculopathy,
27	                          2) myelopathy, 3) unilateral facet fracture, 4) unilateral facet dislocation, and 5) neck pain with MRI showing a ligamen-
28	                          tous STIR signal. Participants were asked about management options and criteria to clear players for RTP using a com-
29	                          bination of multiple-choice and open-ended answers.
30	                          RESULTS A total of 26 physicians from 21 of 32 (66%) teams responded. Anterior surgery was most commonly recom-
31	                          mended for cervical disc herniation causing radiculopathy or myelopathy (73% and 88%, respectively). A rigid cervical
32	                          orthosis was preferred by 68% of experts for initial management of nondisplaced unilateral facet fracture, but single-level
33	                          anterior fusion was preferred by 56% for a unilateral facet dislocation. Common criteria to clear players for RTP with
34	                          cervical disc herniation causing radiculopathy included a normal examination (85%), radiographic fusion postoperatively
35	                          (58%), and pain-free range of motion (50%). Contraindications for RTP included persistent stenosis (35%), instability
36	                          (31%), multilevel fusion (27%), and persistent cord signal change (23%). Additional criteria for RTP in players with facet
37	                          fractures or dislocations included radiographic evidence of fracture healing (32% and 24%, respectively) and normal
38	                          flexion/extension radiographs (24% and 32%, respectively). Finally, for players with isolated ligamentous STIR signal
39	                          changes, resolution of MRI findings was required by 36% of responding physicians prior to RTP.
40	                          CONCLUSIONS Decision-making regarding RTP after cervical spine injuries in professional football players is complex
41	                          and influenced by improvement of symptoms, pain-free range of motion, and radiographic evidence of fusion or fracture
42	                          healing. Respondents preferred anterior cervical discectomy and fusion for disc herniations causing cervical radiculopa-
43	                          thy and myelopathy, rigid orthosis for unilateral facet fractures, and surgery for unilateral facet dislocations. The results
44	                          of this study provide insight into how surgeons serving as consultants to professional football teams may counsel players
45	                          who sustain cervical spine injuries.
