CLINICAL ARTICLE




                          Return to play in professional football players following
                          traumatic cervical spine injury: expert opinions from the
                          National Football League spine surgeons
                          Presented at the 2024 AANS/CNS Joint Section on Disorders of the Spine and Peripheral Nerves

                          *Michael D. White, MD,1 Andrew M. Hersh, MD,2 Carly Weber-Levine, MS,2 Kelly Jiang, MS,2
                          A. Daniel Davidar, MBBS,2 Victoria Bergstein, BA,2 Vikas N. Vattipally, BS,2
                          Scott L. Zuckerman, MD, MPH,3 Allen K. Sills, MD,3 Randall W. Porter, MD,1
                          and Nicholas Theodore, MD2
                          Department of Neurosurgery, Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, Arizona; 2Department of Neurosurgery, Johns Hopkins
                          1

                          University School of Medicine, Baltimore, Maryland; and 3Department of Neurological Surgery, Vanderbilt University Medical
                          Center, Nashville, Tennessee

                          OBJECTIVE There is a paucity of high-quality return-to-play (RTP) data following treatment of cervical spine injuries
                          in contact sports. In this study, the authors gathered insights from National Football League (NFL) team spine surgeon
                          consultants to highlight current practices in treating cervical spine injuries and report decision-making regarding RTP in
                          professional American football players.
                          METHODS A cross-sectional, online survey was distributed to all NFL consulting physicians specializing in the manage-
                          ment of spine injuries. The survey covered the following five clinical vignettes of cervical spine injuries: 1) radiculopathy,
                          2) myelopathy, 3) unilateral facet fracture, 4) unilateral facet dislocation, and 5) neck pain with MRI showing a ligamen-
                          tous STIR signal. Participants were asked about management options and criteria to clear players for RTP using a com-
                          bination of multiple-choice and open-ended answers.
                          RESULTS A total of 26 physicians from 21 of 32 (66%) teams responded. Anterior surgery was most commonly recom-
                          mended for cervical disc herniation causing radiculopathy or myelopathy (73% and 88%, respectively). A rigid cervical
                          orthosis was preferred by 68% of experts for initial management of nondisplaced unilateral facet fracture, but single-level
                          anterior fusion was preferred by 56% for a unilateral facet dislocation. Common criteria to clear players for RTP with
                          cervical disc herniation causing radiculopathy included a normal examination (85%), radiographic fusion postoperatively
                          (58%), and pain-free range of motion (50%). Contraindications for RTP included persistent stenosis (35%), instability
                          (31%), multilevel fusion (27%), and persistent cord signal change (23%). Additional criteria for RTP in players with facet
                          fractures or dislocations included radiographic evidence of fracture healing (32% and 24%, respectively) and normal
                          flexion/extension radiographs (24% and 32%, respectively). Finally, for players with isolated ligamentous STIR signal
                          changes, resolution of MRI findings was required by 36% of responding physicians prior to RTP.
                          CONCLUSIONS Decision-making regarding RTP after cervical spine injuries in professional football players is complex
                          and influenced by improvement of symptoms, pain-free range of motion, and radiographic evidence of fusion or fracture
                          healing. Respondents preferred anterior cervical discectomy and fusion for disc herniations causing cervical radiculopa-
                          thy and myelopathy, rigid orthosis for unilateral facet fractures, and surgery for unilateral facet dislocations. The results
                          of this study provide insight into how surgeons serving as consultants to professional football teams may counsel players
                          who sustain cervical spine injuries.
                          https://thejns.org/doi/abs/10.3171/2024.8.SPINE24421
                          KEYWORDS football; spine; trauma; return to play; cervical; spinal cord injury

   "abstract":"Objective: to report NFL team spine consultants' management and return-to-play decisions after cervical spine injury. Results: 26 physicians from 21 of 32 teams responded. Anterior surgery was most common for disc herniation with radiculopathy (73%) or myelopathy (88%); a rigid orthosis was preferred for nondisplaced facet fracture (68%), and single-level anterior fusion for facet dislocation (56%). Common clearance criteria were a normal examination, pain-free range of motion and radiographic fusion or fracture healing. Conclusions: decisions are complex and vary, and the results show how team consultants may counsel players.",
   "tldr":"NFL team spine consultants mostly favour anterior fusion for disc herniations with radiculopathy or myelopathy and a rigid orthosis for nondisplaced facet fractures. Clearance criteria vary, and most require a normal neurological exam and imaging evidence of healing or fusion.",

Of 26 respondents, one who stopped after the second vignette was excluded from later analyses.",
   "findings":"Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion was the most common choice for disc herniation with radiculopathy (73%) or myelopathy (88%), and the most common time to full professional play was 6 months (42% and 38%). For clearance after disc herniation with radiculopathy, respondents cited a normal examination (85%), radiographic fusion (58%) and pain-free range of motion (50%), and listed persistent stenosis (35%) and instability (31%) as contraindications. Authors describe timing for clearance as highly variable, with 6 to 12 months the common range for facet injuries.",
   "limitations":"The results are expert opinion and self-reported practice from 26 of 49 invited consultants, not player outcomes or a formal consensus. Vignettes are hypothetical and use non-NFL images, and the survey cannot capture all injuries, treatments or clinical nuances. Respondents may read instability and healing on imaging differently, and the authors note the survey is a framework for later Delphi work.",
   "practicalImplications":"Expect team physicians to clear a player for full contact only after a normal neurological examination, pain-free full neck motion and, after surgery, imaging evidence of fusion. Plan around the common 6 to 12 month window for full play after the cited injury types rather than an early return.    "rtp":"The survey shows the criteria NFL spine consultants commonly cite for clearing players after disc herniation, facet injury and ligamentous injury. 18	Purpose Return-to-play (RTP) is an on-going challenge in professional football. Return-to-play related research is increasing.
19	However, it is unknown to what extent the recommendations presented within research are being implemented by professional
20	football teams, and where there are gaps between research and practice. The purposes of this study were (1) to determine if
21	premier-league football teams worldwide follow a RTP continuum, (2) to identify RTP criteria used and (3) to understand
22	how RTP decision-making occurs in applied practice.
23	Methods We sent a structured online survey to practitioners responsible for the RTP programme in 310 professional teams
24	from 34 premier-leagues worldwide. The survey comprised four sections, based on hamstring muscle injury: (1) criteria used
25	throughout RTP phases, (2) the frequency with which progression criteria were achieved, (3) RTP decision-making process
26	and (4) challenges to decision-making.

28	(95%) used a continuum to guide RTP, assessing a combination of clinical, functional and psychological criteria to inform
29	decisions to progress. One-hundred and five (80%) teams reported using a shared decision-making approach considering
30	the input of multiple stakeholders. Team hierarchy, match- and player-related factors were common challenges perceived to
31	influence decision-making.
32	Conclusions General research recommendations for RTP and the beliefs and practices of practitioners appear to match
33	with, the majority of teams assessing functional, clinical and psychological criteria throughout a RTP continuum to inform
34	decision-making which is also shared among key stakeholders. However, specific criteria, metrics and thresholds used, and

Return‑to‑Play Practices Following Hamstring Injury: A Worldwide
Survey of 131 Premier League Football Teams
Gordon Dunlop1,2 · Clare L. Ardern3 · Thor Einar Andersen4 · Colin Lewin5 · Gregory Dupont6 · Ben Ashworth1 ·
Gary O’Driscoll7 · Andrew Rolls8 · Susan Brown2 · Alan McCall1,2

Published online: 8 October 2019
© The Author(s) 2019


Abstract
Purpose Return-to-play (RTP) is an on-going challenge in professional football. Return-to-play related research is increasing.
However, it is unknown to what extent the recommendations presented within research are being implemented by professional
football teams, and where there are gaps between research and practice. The purposes of this study were (1) to determine if
premier-league football teams worldwide follow a RTP continuum, (2) to identify RTP criteria used and (3) to understand
how RTP decision-making occurs in applied practice.
Methods We sent a structured online survey to practitioners responsible for the RTP programme in 310 professional teams
from 34 premier-leagues worldwide. The survey comprised four sections, based on hamstring muscle injury: (1) criteria used
throughout RTP phases, (2) the frequency with which progression criteria were achieved, (3) RTP decision-making process
and (4) challenges to decision-making.
Results One-hundred and thirty-one teams responded with a completed survey (42%). One-hundred and twenty-four teams
(95%) used a continuum to guide RTP, assessing a combination of clinical, functional and psychological criteria to inform
decisions to progress. One-hundred and five (80%) teams reported using a shared decision-making approach considering
the input of multiple stakeholders. Team hierarchy, match- and player-related factors were common challenges perceived to
influence decision-making.
Conclusions General research recommendations for RTP and the beliefs and practices of practitioners appear to match
with, the majority of teams assessing functional, clinical and psychological criteria throughout a RTP continuum to inform
decision-making which is also shared among key stakeholders. However, specific criteria, metrics and thresholds used, and
the specific involvement, dynamics and interactions of staff during decision-making are not clear.

Of these, 131 teams (42%) completed the survey; 124 (95%) reported using a return-to-play continuum with clinical, functional and psychological criteria, and 105 (80%) reported shared decision-making with at least two people involved.    "doi":"10.1007/s40279-019-01199-2",
   "abstract":"Purpose: to determine whether premier-league teams worldwide follow a return-to-play (RTP) continuum, which criteria they use, and how decisions are made after hamstring injury. Methods: a structured online survey sent to practitioners at 310 professional teams from 34 premier leagues. Results: 131 teams responded (42%); 124 (95%) used a continuum assessing clinical, functional and psychological criteria, and 105 (80%) used shared decision-making. Team hierarchy, match and player factors were common perceived challenges. Conclusions: practice appears broadly consistent with general research recommendations, but specific criteria, metrics and thresholds, and the roles of staff in decisions, are unclear.",
   "tldr":"Most professional football teams in this survey used a criteria-based return-to-play continuum with shared decisions after hamstring injury. The specific tests, metrics and thresholds they used were not clear, so the survey cannot show which ones work.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional online survey of 29 items (10 closed, 19 open) across four sections, adapted from a return-to-play continuum model. The survey was piloted for content validity, translated into six languages and sent to 310 teams from 34 leagues between October 2017 and March 2018, with up to three reminders. Open responses were analysed by content analysis, and two authors reviewed the coding.",
   "findings":"124 of 131 responding teams (95%) followed a return-to-play continuum, and 27 (21%) did not report a return-to-performance phase. Absence of pain, hamstring strength, training load and functional performance tests were the most frequently reported top criteria, and 68 teams (52%) reported meeting all criteria before returning to high-speed running. Medical staff were consulted at every phase, but the reported involvement of science staff, coaches and players depended on whether a medical or science practitioner answered the survey.",
   "limitations":"Results are self-reported by 131 of 310 invited teams, so they may not represent non-responding clubs. The survey covers one muscle group and one sport, and it does not describe the metrics or thresholds used, or whether accelerated return led to re-injury. The authors classify the design as level 5 evidence and note that different staff roles gave different accounts of involvement.",
   "practicalImplications":"Teams can use a criteria-based continuum with a shared decision, which the survey shows is common practice. Because the survey found no consistent metrics or thresholds, each team should define and record its own criteria and cut-offs. The survey also suggests the medical and science staff should agree on who is involved in each decision.",
   "athleteDev":"Set progression criteria for each phase (running, team training, match play, return to performance) and track whether they are met. The survey shows training load and functional tests are commonly used, so build a training-load plan into the progression, but no specific thresholds are supported by this study.",
   "rtp":"The survey describes how professional teams make return-to-play decisions after hamstring injury, including a continuum and shared decisions. It cannot show that these criteria or thresholds reduce re-injury, and it cannot be used to set a clearance standard for other muscle groups or injuries."
 }
}

1	                                                                                                                                Original Research
2	
3	
4	Return to Play, Performance, and Economic
5	Analysis of National Football League Players
6	After Lisfranc Injury
7	Varag Abed,* BS, Rebecca Fine,* BA, Rachel Fine,* BA, Gregory S. Hawk,† PhD,
8	Caitlin Conley,* PhD, Cale Jacobs,* PhD, and Austin V. Stone,*‡ MD, PhD
9	Investigation performed at Department of Orthopaedic Surgery and Sports Medicine, University of
10	Kentucky, Lexington, Kentucky, USA
11	
12	Background: A Lisfranc injury can occur to either the ligament or bone, which causes instability when attempting to perform
13	strength and balance maneuvers.
14	Purpose/Hypothesis: The study’s aims were to (1) analyze the return-to-play (RTP) rate and performance level of players in the
15	National Football League (NFL) after Lisfranc injury and (2) determine the economic and financial impact of Lisfranc injuries to the
16	NFL. We hypothesized that there would be a low RTP rate following Lisfranc injury in the NFL.
17	Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
18	Methods: Multiple online public records were used to identify NFL players with Lisfranc injuries between the 2009 and 2020
19	seasons. Players were assessed according to their RTP statistics: snap count, approximate value (AV), games played, and games
20	started. Nonparametric methods were used to compare player statistics before and after injury. Also, player salaries while injured
21	were calculated (in 2022 US dollars after adjusting for inflation) to approximate economic loss for those players who returned to
22	play.
23	Results: A total of 33 NFL athletes sustained a Lisfranc injury during the study period. Most Lisfranc injuries were experienced by
24	offensive linemen (n ¼ 8; 24.2%), followed by running backs (n ¼ 7; 21.2%). Overall 27 players (81.8%) returned to play after injury
25	at a median of 11.0 months (IQR, 10.2-11.8 months). There were no significant differences between pre- and postinjury snap
26	counts or number of games played and started. In terms of player performance, there was a statistically significant decrease in AV
27	at 1 year postinjury (median [IQR], 6.0 [4.0-10.0] preinjury vs 5.0 [2.5-7.5] postinjury; P ¼ .022). The overall cost of recovery
28	amounted to $104.7 million, with quarterbacks (n ¼ 4) accounting for the greatest cost at $32.6 million. The next 2 most expensive
29	positions were offensive and defensive linemen (n ¼ 5 each) at $19.4 million each.
30	Conclusion: Our results did not support the hypothesis, as the RTP rate for NFL athletes sustaining Lisfranc injuries was 81.8%.

32	accounted for almost one-third of expenses while constituting only 14.8% of injuries.

Original Research


Return to Play, Performance, and Economic
Analysis of National Football League Players
After Lisfranc Injury
Varag Abed,* BS, Rebecca Fine,* BA, Rachel Fine,* BA, Gregory S. Hawk,† PhD,
Caitlin Conley,* PhD, Cale Jacobs,* PhD, and Austin V. Stone,*‡ MD, PhD
Investigation performed at Department of Orthopaedic Surgery and Sports Medicine, University of
Kentucky, Lexington, Kentucky, USA

Background: A Lisfranc injury can occur to either the ligament or bone, which causes instability when attempting to perform
strength and balance maneuvers.
Purpose/Hypothesis: The study’s aims were to (1) analyze the return-to-play (RTP) rate and performance level of players in the
National Football League (NFL) after Lisfranc injury and (2) determine the economic and financial impact of Lisfranc injuries to the
NFL. We hypothesized that there would be a low RTP rate following Lisfranc injury in the NFL.
Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
Methods: Multiple online public records were used to identify NFL players with Lisfranc injuries between the 2009 and 2020
seasons. Players were assessed according to their RTP statistics: snap count, approximate value (AV), games played, and games
started. Nonparametric methods were used to compare player statistics before and after injury. Also, player salaries while injured
were calculated (in 2022 US dollars after adjusting for inflation) to approximate economic loss for those players who returned to
play.
Results: A total of 33 NFL athletes sustained a Lisfranc injury during the study period. Most Lisfranc injuries were experienced by
offensive linemen (n ¼ 8; 24.2%), followed by running backs (n ¼ 7; 21.2%). Overall 27 players (81.8%) returned to play after injury
at a median of 11.0 months (IQR, 10.2-11.8 months). There were no significant differences between pre- and postinjury snap
counts or number of games played and started. In terms of player performance, there was a statistically significant decrease in AV
at 1 year postinjury (median [IQR], 6.0 [4.0-10.0] preinjury vs 5.0 [2.5-7.5] postinjury; P ¼ .022). The overall cost of recovery
amounted to $104.7 million, with quarterbacks (n ¼ 4) accounting for the greatest cost at $32.6 million. The next 2 most expensive
positions were offensive and defensive linemen (n ¼ 5 each) at $19.4 million each.
Conclusion: Our results did not support the hypothesis, as the RTP rate for NFL athletes sustaining Lisfranc injuries was 81.8%.
This injury was associated with a significant decrease in AV 1 year postinjury. In terms of economic impact, quarterbacks
accounted for almost one-third of expenses while constituting only 14.8% of injuries.
Keywords: Lisfranc; NFL; National Football League; foot

Approximate value fell significantly in the first season back (median 6.0 to 5.0, P = .022), and the authors estimate $104.7 million (2022 US dollars) in salary cost for games missed by returning players.",

   "year":2023,

   "doi":"10.1177/23259671231159935",
   "abstract":"Background: a Lisfranc injury to the ligament or bone causes instability during strength and balance tasks. Purpose: to analyse return to play (RTP) and performance after Lisfranc injury in the NFL, and to estimate the economic impact. Study design: case series, level 4. Methods: NFL players with Lisfranc injuries from 2009 to 2020 were identified from public records; snap counts, approximate value (AV), games played and started were compared before and after injury, and salary loss was estimated. Results: 33 players were identified, 27 (81.8%) returned at a median of 11.0 months, AV fell significantly at 1 year (P = .022), and cost of recovery was $104.7 million, with quarterbacks accounting for $32.6 million. Conclusion: the RTP rate was higher than hypothesised, with a significant AV decrease at 1 year and quarterbacks responsible for almost one-third of costs.",
   "tldr":"Most NFL players with a Lisfranc injury (27 of 33) returned to play at about 11 months, but their approximate value fell in the first season back. The salary cost of missed games was large, driven mainly by quarterbacks.",
   "methods":"Case series of NFL players with Lisfranc injuries, identified by cross-referencing official injury reports, press releases and sports websites, with each case confirmed by at least two sources. Performance data came from Pro Football Reference for 3 seasons before and after return, and non-parametric Wilcoxon tests were used. Salary loss was calculated from Spotrac earnings divided by 17 weeks, multiplied by games missed, and adjusted to 2022 dollars.",
   "findings":"Of 33 players, 27 (81.8%) returned to play at a median of 11.0 months, and 23 of 26 operated players were still active two seasons later. Snap counts and games played and started did not change significantly, but AV fell at 1 year (median 6.0 to 5.0; P = .022), and the 3-year AV change was not significant (P = .080). The estimated salary cost of missed games for returning players was $104.7 million, with quarterbacks at $32.6 million from four players.",
   "limitations":"Players were identified from public sources, so unreported injuries are missing. The AV metric is not validated, and per-position groups are very small, so the study is underpowered. Injury type (soft tissue or bony), surgery details and rehabilitation were not assessed, and preseason and playoff games and the cost of travel and rehabilitation were excluded from the cost analysis.",
   "practicalImplications":"Counsel players that most returned to NFL play after about 11 months, but plan for a drop in performance in the first season back. Use the cost estimate to inform roster and contract planning, while recognising that it reflects salary for games missed, not a complete financial cost.",
   "athleteDev":"Build the return-to-performance plan around role-specific output, not only time to first game. Across returning players, AV fell by about 23% and snap counts by about 9% in the first season back, though these position estimates rest on 2 to 4 players each.",
   "rtp":"Of players who were injured, 81.8% returned to at least one regular-season snap at a median of 11.0 months, which is a minimal definition of return. The study cannot show whether operative or nonoperative care, injury type or rehabilitation changes this outcome, so it cannot set a clearance standard for a specific case."
 }
}

The study cannot show whether operative or nonoperative care, injury type or rehabilitation changes this outcome, so it cannot set a clearance standard for a specific case."

16	Background: A precise and consistent definition of return to sport (RTS) after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is lacking, and
17	there is controversy surrounding the process of returning patients to sport and their previous activity level.
18	Purpose: The aim of the Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group was to provide a clear definition of RTS
19	after ACL injury and a description of the RTS continuum as well as provide clinical guidance on RTS testing and decision-making.
20	Study Design: Consensus statement.
21	Methods: An international, multidisciplinary group of ACL experts convened as part of a consensus meeting. Consensus
22	statements were developed using a modified Delphi method. Literature review was performed to report the supporting
23	evidence.
24	Results: Key points include that RTS is characterized by achievement of the preinjury level of sport and involves a criteria-based
25	progression from return to participation to RTS and, ultimately, return to performance. Purely time-based RTS decision-making
26	should be abandoned. Progression occurs along an RTS continuum, with decision-making by a multidisciplinary group that
27	incorporates objective physical examination data and validated and peer-reviewed RTS tests, which should involve functional
28	assessment as well as psychological readiness. Consideration should be given to biological healing, contextual factors, and
29	concomitant injuries.
30	Conclusion: The resultant consensus statements and scientific rationale aim to inform the reader of the complex process
31	of RTS after ACL injury that occurs along a dynamic continuum. Research is needed to determine the ideal RTS test
32	battery, the best implementation of psychological readiness testing, and methods for the biological assessment of healing
33	and recovery.

Consensus Statement


Return to Sport After Anterior
Cruciate Ligament Injury
Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return
to Sport Consensus Group
Sean J. Meredith,* MD, Thomas Rauer, MD, Terese L. Chmielewski, PT, PhD, SCS,
Christian Fink, MD, Theresa Diermeier, MD, Benjamin B. Rothrauff, MD, PhD,
Eleonor Svantesson, MD, Eric Hamrin Senorski, PT, PhD, MSc,
Timothy E. Hewett, PhD, FACSM, Seth L. Sherman, MD, Bryson P. Lesniak, MD,
and the Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group
Investigation performed at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center,
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA

Background: A precise and consistent definition of return to sport (RTS) after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is lacking, and
there is controversy surrounding the process of returning patients to sport and their previous activity level.
Purpose: The aim of the Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group was to provide a clear definition of RTS
after ACL injury and a description of the RTS continuum as well as provide clinical guidance on RTS testing and decision-making.
Study Design: Consensus statement.
Methods: An international, multidisciplinary group of ACL experts convened as part of a consensus meeting. Consensus
statements were developed using a modified Delphi method. Literature review was performed to report the supporting
evidence.
Results: Key points include that RTS is characterized by achievement of the preinjury level of sport and involves a criteria-based
progression from return to participation to RTS and, ultimately, return to performance. Purely time-based RTS decision-making
should be abandoned. Progression occurs along an RTS continuum, with decision-making by a multidisciplinary group that
incorporates objective physical examination data and validated and peer-reviewed RTS tests, which should involve functional
assessment as well as psychological readiness. Consideration should be given to biological healing, contextual factors, and
concomitant injuries.
Conclusion: The resultant consensus statements and scientific rationale aim to inform the reader of the complex process
of RTS after ACL injury that occurs along a dynamic continuum. Research is needed to determine the ideal RTS test
battery, the best implementation of psychological readiness testing, and methods for the biological assessment of healing
and recovery.
Keywords: anterior cruciate ligament; return to sport; rehabilitation; sports medicine

Of 11 statements, consensus was reached that return to sport means regaining the preinjury level of sport, that purely time-based decisions should be abandoned (26 of 26), and that decisions need objective examination data (26 of 26), a validated test (23 of 26) and a validated psychological readiness measure (22 of 26). Coach involvement in the clearance decision did not reach consensus (7 of 26).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The statements are expert opinion built on a single MEDLINE search covering 5 to 10 years, and the authors did not use a formal systematic review. The authors state that the ideal test battery, psychological tools and biological healing measures remain unresolved.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the statements as a validated return-to-sport protocol with fixed criteria, when the authors describe them as consensus principles and say the exact test battery and thresholds still need research.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Meredith SJ, Rauer T, Chmielewski TL, et al. Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group. Orthop J Sports Med 2020;8(6):2325967120930829.",
   "doi":"10.1177/2325967120930829",
   "abstract":"Background: a precise and consistent definition of return to sport (RTS) after ACL injury is lacking. Purpose: to define RTS, describe the RTS continuum and give guidance on RTS testing and decisions. Study design: consensus statement. Methods: an international multidisciplinary group used a modified Delphi method, with a literature review. Results: RTS is achieved when the preinjury level of sport is reached, through criteria-based progression from return to participation to RTS and return to performance. Purely time-based decisions should be abandoned; decisions should be made by a multidisciplinary group using objective examination data and validated, peer-reviewed RTS tests that include functional and psychological assessment, and should consider biological healing, context and concomitant injuries. Conclusion: research is needed on the ideal test battery, psychological readiness testing and biological assessment of healing.",
   "tldr":"Return to sport after ACL injury should mean regaining the preinjury level of sport, reached through criteria-based stages. Time alone should not decide clearance, and the decision should use examination data, validated tests and psychological readiness.",
   "methods":"International consensus group of 26 ACL experts convened at a symposium in June 2019. A modified Delphi process ran three rounds (internet survey, structured in-person discussion and a final vote), with 80% agreement set in advance as consensus. Two liaisons completed a MEDLINE search (June 2019; anterior cruciate ligament, return to sport and return to play; 5 to 10 years) to support the statements.",
   "findings":"Consensus was reached on 11 statements. Return to sport was defined as the preinjury level of sport (24 of 26, 92%), and purely time-based decisions should be abandoned (26 of 26). Objective physical examination was required (26 of 26), with validated tests (23 of 26) and a validated psychological readiness scale (22 of 26). Cited data from the Delaware-Oslo cohort show that patients who passed a criteria-based test at 6 months returned to their previous level at 81% (1 year) and 84% (2 years).",
   "limitations":"The statements are consensus opinion built from an expert panel and a single MEDLINE search, not a systematic review or meta-analysis. The authors note that the best test battery, the psychological tools to use, and how to assess biological healing are not yet known. Some statements, such as the role of the coach, did not reach consensus, and the cited RTS outcomes come mainly from one cohort.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use criteria-based progression through return to participation, return to sport and return to performance, with a documented clearance by the health care provider before unrestricted training. Include objective examination, a validated test battery and a psychological readiness measure, and consider contextual factors such as position, sport and concomitant injury. Avoid clearing an athlete on time alone, and treat RTS before about 6 months as likely high risk.",
   "athleteDev":"Apply the RTS continuum to sport-specific training: clear unrestricted training first, then full participation in practice, then competition, with serial testing at each stage. Measure readiness with objective tests of strength, hop and movement quality before progressing, and do not use the calendar as the trigger.",
   "rtp":"The statements describe a criteria-based return to sport after ACL injury, requiring objective examination, a validated test battery and psychological readiness, with time used as a guide to graft healing rather than the decision. The paper cannot specify the exact test battery or thresholds, and it cannot be used as a validated clearance protocol or as a guarantee of return to the preinjury level."

Article history:                                        Background: Hamstring strain injuries are the most common type of injury in elite football and are
Received 22 March 2022                                  associated with a high risk of reinjury, particularly those involving the intramuscular tendon (IMT).
Received in revised form                                Limited information is available regarding the rehabilitation and return to sport (RTS) processes
25 May 2022
                                                        following such injuries. This case study describes the clinical presentation of an elite football player
Accepted 26 May 2022
                                                        following IMT hamstring injury, their on- and off-pitch rehabilitation alongside performance monitoring
                                                        throughout RTS and beyond.
Keywords:
                                                        Case scenario: An elite football player suffered a grade 2c hamstring injury during an English Premier
Elite football
Rehabilitation
                                                        League (EPL) match. The player underwent early post-injury management, alongside progressive off-
Hamstring injury                                        pitch physical preparation. The ‘control-chaos continuum’ was used as a framework for on-pitch reha-
Intramuscular tendon                                    bilitation to prepare the player for a return to full team training and competition. Objective and sub-
Performance monitoring                                  jective markers of the player's response to progressive on- and off-pitch loading were monitored
Load response                                           throughout RTS and beyond.
                                                        Outcomes: The player returned to on-pitch rehabilitation after 11 days, to full team training having
                                                        achieved weekly pre-injury chronic running load outputs after 35 days and played in the EPL 40 days
                                                        post-injury. The player did not suffer reinjury for the rest of the EPL season.
                                                        Conclusion: An understanding the unique structural and mechanical properties of the IMT, alongside
                                                        expected RTS timeframes are important to inform rehabilitation and decision-making processes post-
                                                        injury. Performance and frequent load-response monitoring throughout RTS and beyond, in conjunc-
                                                        tion with practitioner experience and effective communication are critical in facilitating effective RTS and
                                                        reduce risk of reinjury following IMT injury.

   "doi":"10.1016/j.ptsp.2022.05.013",
   "abstract":"Background: hamstring strains are the most common injury in elite football and carry a high reinjury risk, especially when the intramuscular tendon (IMT) is involved, and rehabilitation data for these injuries are limited. Case scenario: an elite player suffered a grade 2c hamstring injury in an EPL match and was managed with early care, progressive off-pitch physical preparation and the control-chaos continuum for on-pitch rehabilitation, with objective and subjective load-response monitoring. Outcomes: on-pitch rehabilitation at 11 days, full team training at 35 days, match play at 40 days, and no reinjury for the rest of the season. Conclusion: knowledge of the IMT and expected return timeframes, with performance and load-response monitoring, communication and practitioner experience, may help to guide return to sport.",
   "tldr":"A single elite player with an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury returned to full team training at 35 days and played at 40 days without reinjury. Isometric strength monitoring and load tracking guided each step, but this is one case.",
   "methods":"Single case report of one 23-year-old male player managed by the club's medical and sports science staff. Care followed a modified return-to-sport continuum with the control-chaos continuum for on-pitch work. Isometric posterior chain peak force (unilateral test on a force platform at 1000 Hz) and interlimb asymmetry were measured weekly and before most training sessions. GPS load and MRI and ultrasound were used at set points, and the player gave informed consent.",
   "findings":"Interlimb asymmetry in isometric posterior chain peak force fell below 10% by day 11, and the player reached his pre-injury weekly running load before full team training at day 35. He then played as a substitute for about 40 to 45 minutes in five matches and started one 90-minute match, where his high-speed running was 1.26 times his typical pre-injury game load, with no reinjury for the rest of the season. Authors note that the largest force decline came about 48 hours after match play, and it was symmetrical across both limbs.",
   "limitations":"Findings come from one player, one club and one injury, without a control group or a validated threshold for IPC asymmetry. The authors state that the timeline and the monitoring approach may not transfer to other players or clubs, and that the link between the monitoring and reinjury risk is unproven.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use an isometric strength test and load data before each stage of return, and combine them with pain response and player feedback. Consider an early phase of controlled loading and partial team involvement, as the authors describe, but expect the timeline to vary by injury and player. Keep monitoring after return to play, since the authors judged the reinjury risk after this injury type to be high.",
   "athleteDev":"Use the control-chaos continuum to build back to match demands: progress high-speed running and maximal speed exposure against the match demand, and check strength asymmetry the morning after sessions. The case suggests that matching training volume to the player's pre-injury weekly running load was a practical target before full team training.",
   "rtp":"The case describes one player who returned to team training at 35 days and to match play at 40 days after an intramuscular tendon hamstring injury, without reinjury for the season. It cannot set a return-to-play timeline for this injury, because the authors recommend an individual approach and the case involves no comparison."
 }
}

113   sports. Griffith et al identified several factors in return to sports after upper extremity surgery: time,

114   muscle strength, range of motion, pain, successful sport specific testing, proprioception, patient-

115   surgeon agreement on RTS clearance, radiographic healing. Third, the readiness for an athlete to be

116   able to return to competition is dependent on type of sport and position in the game. However, there is

117   to date no consensus on the return to sports criteria to use in clinical practice. [32] In the study of

593	
594	157           The main finding of this review is the high return to sports rate (95.3%) for athletes
595	
596	158   undergoing distal biceps tendon repair and 81.8% returned to the same level. The overall functional
597	
598	159   outcomes were good and comparable to the unoperated arm or matched controls. The time to return to
599

601	
602	161   season. This should be discussed with the athlete (and potentially the coach) in order to manage
603	
604	162   expectations. Based on the results of this review, there are several factors that can be associated with a
605

148   and after subgroup analysis, with the defensive backs (n = 5) having a statistically significant shorter

149   career length following surgery compared to matched controls.[21]


150


151   Complications


152           Relatively few complications were seen in the reviewed studies. Of all studies, only one

153   complication (0.01%) needed surgical intervention: a suture anchor migrated. In one study, two

154   patients had postoperative heterotopic ossifications of the tendon at the site of attachment to the radial

155
                                                                        of
      tuberosity, but it did not affect their range of motion or functional outcome.[20]


                                                                 ro
                                                      e- p
                                              Pr
                                  na l
                   Jour




                                                                                                                 9
 156   Discussion

157           The main finding of this review is the high return to sports rate (95.3%) for athletes

158   undergoing distal biceps tendon repair and 81.8% returned to the same level. The overall functional

159   outcomes were good and comparable to the unoperated arm or matched controls. The time to return to

160   competition is relatively long (38.8 weeks) and, depending on the sport, not possible within the same

161   season. This should be discussed with the athlete (and potentially the coach) in order to manage

162   expectations. Based on the results of this review, there are several factors that can be associated with a

163   decreased likelihood and increased duration to sports. These factors include injury on the dominant

164
                                                                         of
      arm, single incision approach, suture anchor technique and a longer duration from injury to surgery.


165
                                                                  ro
              Return to sports data, such as the time needed to return, are an important measurement of the

166                                                   e- p
      effectiveness of the rehabilitation and treatment regimens and multiple factors are involved. The

167   recovery of the repair of the distal biceps tendon is relatively long and in case of a NFL player, it is

168
                                               Pr
      unlikely that the player returns within the same season.[5] McGinnis found that the injured players

169

170
                                   na
      were relatively further along in their career and this could have impacted the return to play rate and

                                      l
      level.[3] Additionally, NFL players have a relatively short professional career in general and it could

171

172
                   Jo
      be possible that it is detrimental to miss a season because of an injury. Several of the included studies

                     ur
      documented flexion or supination strength deficits, but it did not prove to be of clinical importance in

173   the return to sports rate or level.


174           In most sports, athletes require the primary use of the dominant arm and if that arm is injured,

175   the time to return to play, especially at the same level, can be prolonged. Multiple studies have

176   demonstrated equivalent of isometric strength in comparison to the contralateral arm following distal

177   biceps tendon repair. However, there is a probability that these results are biased, especially in athletes

178   that work with their dominant arm, the difference in (baseline) strength could be altered.[25,33]


179           Gowd et al mentioned an increased duration to return to sports with a single incision approach.

180   However, a prior prospective clinical trial, that compared the single-incision approach using suture

181   anchors to the double-incision technique using transosseous tunnels, did not find statistically
                                                                                                                 10
 182   significant differences in outcomes. Based on the results of this review we cannot conclude if this was

183   of influence on the return to sports rate.[17,25] The decreased likelihood to return to sports following a

184   suture anchor technique was also mentioned as a factor, but differences are small and likely not

185   clinically relevant.[6] Numerous factors influence the strength of a soft–tissue-to-bone fixation

186   construct, including tissue quality, implant strength, contact area and pressure, and tensioning.[34] In

187   the current literature there are indications that more reruptures occur following the suture anchor

188   technique.[35] Several biomechanical studies have shown that the cortical button technique, has a

189   greater load to failure.[29] To date there is no agreement on the optimal surgical approach or

190   technique.[17]
                                                                         of
191                                                               ro
              The overall complication rate in this study was 0.01%, one patient had a migration of a suture

192

193
                                                       e-
      anchor. Heterotopic ossifications were seen in two athletes, but not symptomatic and were therefore

                                                          p
      not seen as a complication.[16] In other studies, complication rates of 20.4 – 24.5% are mentioned,

194

195
                                               Pr
      and a major complication rate of 4.6%.[10,17] The low complication rate in the included studies could

      indicate a bias, as athletes that had complications could have been lost in the follow-up. None of the

196                                na
      studies mentioned the reason why athletes did not return to sports or to the same level.
                                      l
197

198
                   Jo
              The timing from injury to surgery was reported to be a factor for an increased duration for the


                     ur
      return to play. Evidence has shown that early distal biceps repair (performed within 4 weeks of injury)

199   does result in statistically significant better outcomes, but the return to previous activity was similar

200   for all patients.[13] However, one can argue that the sooner the athletes are operated, the sooner they

201   will be able to return to play.


202           An adequate rehabilitation protocol is an important factor for the rate and time of the return to

203   play in general. To date, the rehabilitation protocols are not evidence based, and seemingly based on

204   preference of the publishing surgeon and highly variable.[18,36] In recent studies a trend is seen from

205   longer immobilization periods and slower progression of weight bearing and strength building towards

206   early ROM and aggressive muscle rehabilitation.[18,37] In a few studies, immediate mobilization, as

207   tolerated, showed good clinical results without an increase in complications.[38] Although these were


                                                                                                                  11
 208   not comparative studies, early loading of the tendon seems to be safe. Early active mobilization may

209   improve the time to return to sports, but further research is necessary.


210           A limitation to this review is the relatively small patient group, due to relatively few clinical

211   studies in athletes that included the assessment of the return to sports. The heterogeneity in reporting

212   outcomes, the retrospective aspect of the studies, and little information about surgical techniques or

213   rehabilitation protocols are other limitations to this review. The different type of sports (NFL and

214   weightlifting) might also have an impact on the timing and return to sports. The studies were not

215   controlled for potential cofounders including concomitant injuries, trades, personal obligations,

216                                                                      of
      coaching changes, or changes in team setup that may have impacted both the case and control cohorts.

217                                                               ro
      These factors will likely confound the findings of a decreased postinjury career length and games per

218

219
                                                      e-
      season. Lastly, differences in postoperative management could be of influence on the return to

                                                         p
      previous level of play and complications. It is necessary to elucidate whether early ROM and an

220

221
                                              Pr
      aggressive rehabilitation protocol improves the return to sports. A standardized protocol for reporting

      outcome measures, including return to sports rate, timing and strength measurements, is necessary for

222                               na
      further research. All these factors can be important for the timing and rate of the return to play to the
                                     l
223   same level.

                    Jour




                                                                                                                  12
 224   Conclusion

225             To conclude, 95.3% of the athletes with repair of the distal biceps tendon returned to sports

226   and 81.8% to the same preinjury level of competition. The functional outcomes following surgery

227   were good and generally not clinically different compared to matched athletes. The average time to

228   return to sports was 38.8 (range 27.6 – 50) weeks, depending on type of sport. The relatively long

229   rehabilitation period before returning to competition is important to discuss with the athlete in order to

230   manage expectations. Early mobilization following distal biceps tendon repair might have a positive

231   influence on the return to sports rate. Future research is necessary to compare surgical techniques,

232
                                                                         of
      rehabilitation program and functional outcomes in order to draw conclusions about factors on return to

233   sports.                                                     ro
